screens.title: Naming Classes and Files
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how naming shapes the clarity of a codebase. Good names are not cosmetic: they communicate responsibility, scope, and the role a class or file plays in the domain. We treat classes as nouns or noun phrases, and modules as containers named for their primary content. You will see examples of clear names like UserProfile and OrderFulfillmentService, and contrast them with vague anti-patterns like DataHelper or Utils. We'll also cover interfaces and abstract types: choosing names that read like contracts rather than implementations. Naming conventions for files and packages are part of the same design choice — consistent snake_case for Python modules, and folders that group related behaviors. By the end you'll be able to rename classes, reorganize files, and explain why a name indicates a single responsibility. A quick example: renaming ProductProcessor to ProductService clarifies it offers product-related operations rather than being a catch-all processor. Think of names as the first, most honest documentation of your code. How would you name a class that only formats email content?

screens.title: Classes as Nouns
screens.narratorSegment: A clear starting point is to treat classes as nouns or noun phrases. This is not a stylistic preference but a semantic mapping: classes represent entities, concepts, or cohesive services inside your domain. Naming a class User or Product establishes what the object is; UserProfile suggests the data associated with a user and the behaviors that relate to that profile. That clarity makes reading code almost like reading a sentence. A concrete example: a class named Order will likely hold order data and simple methods; OrderFulfillmentService signals a service that performs multiple steps to complete an order. A common misconception is that longer names are bad; in fact, longer, precise names often beat short, vague names because they reduce ambiguity. Another misconception is that a class must always be a single data holder; sometimes classes represent processes or services, and the noun phrase should reflect that role, for example CsvParser or ConfigurationLoader. To test a name, try to express its responsibility in one short sentence. If you struggle, the name probably hides additional responsibilities and the class may need refactoring. Takeaway: prefer clear nouns that match responsibility and avoid abbreviations that obscure meaning.

screens.title: Good vs Bad Class Names
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing examples is one of the fastest ways to learn naming discipline. Consider 'OrderProcessor' versus 'OrderFulfillmentService'. Both imply work related to orders, but the latter communicates a multi-step responsibility — fulfillment — while the former is ambiguous about what processing means. Another common pair is 'FileUtil' versus 'CsvParser'. FileUtil leaves open what files and what utilities; CsvParser immediately tells you the file format and the task. A concrete diagnostic is to ask: who would call this class and for what reason? If the answer is not immediate, the name is likely too broad. Watch out for anti-patterns such as 'Manager', 'Helper', or 'Util' appearing without context. These suffixes often signal accumulated responsibilities. A productive misconception to check is assuming 'Service' is always bad — it is not. Service is appropriate when a class encapsulates a stateless set of operations or a domain service, but it should be paired with a clear domain noun, like PaymentService or NotificationService. Closing question: when you read a class name, can you describe its single responsibility in one sentence? Good vs Bad Class Names means specific names reduce ambiguity. use domain nouns and precise task words rather than generic suffixes.. In practical terms, spotting vagueness and improving intent with examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: The Problem with Manager / Helper / Util
screens.narratorSegment: Suffixes like Manager, Helper, and Util are common anti-patterns because they often hide multiple responsibilities and become catch-alls for unrelated methods. A file named FileUtil could contain CSV parsing, JSON serialization, string trimming, and logging helpers. When a name is that broad, it becomes a maintenance burden: developers add more unrelated functions rather than finding the right abstraction. A concrete example: DataHelper with methods load_csv, save_json, and query_db probably mixes IO, serialization, and data access. A better approach is to split these responsibilities into CsvSerializer, JsonSerializer, and DbConnector or Repository. Another misconception is thinking it's fine to have shared utilities to avoid duplication. Duplication is not the only problem — unclear ownership and hidden dependencies are worse. Splitting responsibilities makes testing, reuse, and documentation straightforward. Use the Single Responsibility Principle as your naming guide: if a name cannot be expressed as a single responsibility, favor decomposition. Takeaway: short generic suffixes often mean you'll need to refactor; prefer specific nouns and task words. screens.title: Naming Interfaces and Abstract Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Interfaces and abstract classes represent contracts or blueprints. Their names should make that role explicit so implementers and callers understand the expectation. In languages like Java or C# an 'I' prefix is conventional — for example IUserService or IRepository — because it signals an interface rather than a concrete class. In Python, explicit interfaces are less common; abstract base classes can be prefixed with Abstract or simply named as the role they define, such as PaymentGateway, where documentation or module structure clarifies that it is not a concrete implementation. A common misconception is to name an interface like 'PaymentServiceImpl' or to hide its contract in a concrete-sounding name. Instead, choose names that emphasize behavior and expectation, not the implementation. For example, NotificationService can be an interface that has implementations like EmailNotificationSender or SmsNotificationSender. This naming makes substitution and testing easier because developers can swap implementations when dependencies expect the contract. Takeaway: name interfaces for the role and name implementations for the mechanism. Naming Interfaces and Abstract Classes means interfaces and abstracts should convey contractual behavior; implementations should convey mechanism and detail.. In practical terms, make contracts obvious, not confusing implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: File and Module Naming for Python
screens.narratorSegment: File and module naming ties directly to discovery and import ergonomics in a project. In Python, the conventional style is snake_case for file names, so a class UserProfile belongs in user_profile dot P Y file. Follow these steps when naming or refactoring a module: first, identify the module's primary responsibility — the single class or cohesive set of functions that most represent the file. Second, name the file after that primary element, using snake_case. Third, avoid embedding version numbers or environment details in file names; source control tracks versions. Fourth, if a file grows beyond a single responsibility, split it into focused modules and organize them into a package directory named for the domain area, for example auth or payments. A practical misconception is thinking filenames should mirror class casing. In Python they should not: classes use CamelCase while filenames use snake_case. Takeaway: consistent module names speed navigation and reduce accidental imports from the wrong file. screens.title: When to Rename or Split
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding when to rename or split a class or file can be guided by a short checklist. First, ask whether the name describes a single responsibility. If you cannot write a one-sentence responsibility description, plan a refactor. Second, check call sites: are callers confused about what the class does? Third, inspect the methods: do they belong together conceptually, or do they span IO, parsing, and persistence? If the latter, split along those concerns. Fourth, consider tests and dependencies: renaming is simpler when you have tests that signal behavior has not changed. A common misconception is to avoid small refactors for fear of churn; small, frequent renames that improve clarity are usually worth the short effort. For larger changes, consider deprecation shims to preserve public imports. The closing takeaway is simple: prefer names that narrow expected behavior and split files when multiple responsibilities appear. This keeps the codebase navigable and reduces accidental coupling. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how naming shapes the clarity of a codebase. Good names are not cosmetic: they communicate responsibility, scope, and the role a class or file plays in the domain. We treat classes as nouns or noun phrases, and modules as containers named for their primary content. You will see examples of clear names like UserProfile and OrderFulfillmentService, and contrast them with vague anti-patterns like DataHelper or Utils. We'll also cover interfaces and abstract types: choosing names that read like contracts rather than implementations. Naming conventions for files and packages are part of the same design choice — consistent snake_case for Python modules, and folders that group related behaviors. By the end you'll be able to rename classes, reorganize files, and explain why a name indicates a single responsibility. A quick example: renaming ProductProcessor to ProductService clarifies it offers product-related operations rather than being a catch-all processor. Think of names as the first, most honest documentation of your code. How would you name a class that only formats email content?

By the end of these screens you will confidently produce and critique names for classes, interfaces, and files. First, practice formulating clear, descriptive class names that map to single responsibilities. For example, move from generic 'Manager' to 'OrderFulfillmentService' when the class orchestrates order completion. Second, distinguish good and bad naming patterns: you will learn to spot vague suffixes like Manager, Helper, Util, and Service when they lack context. Third, name interfaces and abstract classes so they read as contracts — in some languages an 'I' prefix or an 'Abstract' prefix helps, while in Python the abstract concept can be conveyed by the role name or documentation. Finally, apply consistent file and module naming so files match their main class or function and use the project's standard casing. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can self-assess. You will practice these on a small e-commerce codebase and leave with a checklist you can reuse.

These objectives focus on application. You will practice renaming classes, updating file names, and reorganizing package structure so each module maps to a clear purpose. A concrete activity will take you through a small e-commerce project where you rename DataHelper to CsvJsonSerializer and move models into a dedicated models package. We will also exercise common-sense naming choices for services and repositories so that other developers can infer behavior without reading implementation. Along the way you will learn to question names that signal a 'God' class or a utilities grab-bag, and apply simple tests: can you explain the class responsibility in one sentence? If not, the name likely needs change. These skills reduce cognitive load in code reviews and make refactors safer because names narrow the expected behavior before you even open a file.

A clear starting point is to treat classes as nouns or noun phrases. This is not a stylistic preference but a semantic mapping: classes represent entities, concepts, or cohesive services inside your domain. Naming a class User or Product establishes what the object is; UserProfile suggests the data associated with a user and the behaviors that relate to that profile. That clarity makes reading code almost like reading a sentence. A concrete example: a class named Order will likely hold order data and simple methods; OrderFulfillmentService signals a service that performs multiple steps to complete an order. A common misconception is that longer names are bad; in fact, longer, precise names often beat short, vague names because they reduce ambiguity. Another misconception is that a class must always be a single data holder; sometimes classes represent processes or services, and the noun phrase should reflect that role, for example CsvParser or ConfigurationLoader. To test a name, try to express its responsibility in one short sentence. If you struggle, the name probably hides additional responsibilities and the class may need refactoring. Takeaway: prefer clear nouns that match responsibility and avoid abbreviations that obscure meaning.

Comparing examples is one of the fastest ways to learn naming discipline. Consider 'OrderProcessor' versus 'OrderFulfillmentService'. Both imply work related to orders, but the latter communicates a multi-step responsibility — fulfillment — while the former is ambiguous about what processing means. Another common pair is 'FileUtil' versus 'CsvParser'. FileUtil leaves open what files and what utilities; CsvParser immediately tells you the file format and the task. A concrete diagnostic is to ask: who would call this class and for what reason? If the answer is not immediate, the name is likely too broad. Watch out for anti-patterns such as 'Manager', 'Helper', or 'Util' appearing without context. These suffixes often signal accumulated responsibilities. A productive misconception to check is assuming 'Service' is always bad — it is not. Service is appropriate when a class encapsulates a stateless set of operations or a domain service, but it should be paired with a clear domain noun, like PaymentService or NotificationService. Closing question: when you read a class name, can you describe its single responsibility in one sentence? Suffixes like Manager, Helper, and Util are common anti-patterns because they often hide multiple responsibilities and become catch-alls for unrelated methods. When a name is that broad, it becomes a maintenance burden: developers add more unrelated functions rather than finding the right abstraction. A concrete example: DataHelper with methods load_csv, save_json, and query_db probably mixes IO, serialization, and data access. Third, inspect the methods: do they belong together conceptually, or do they span IO, parsing, and persistence? If the latter, split along those concerns. Fourth, consider tests and dependencies: renaming is simpler when you have tests that signal behavior has not changed. A common misconception is to avoid small refactors for fear of churn; small, frequent renames that improve clarity are usually worth the short effort. For larger changes, consider deprecation shims to preserve public imports. The closing takeaway is simple: prefer names that narrow expected behavior and split files when multiple responsibilities appear. This keeps the codebase navigable and reduces accidental coupling. This lesson lists common naming mistakes and practical ways to avoid them. First, overly generic names like Processor or Handler are ambiguous; fix them by naming the specific domain action or object, for example CsvParser instead of FileProcessor. Second, redundant naming such as UserClass or ItemModel repeats type information; simply use User or Item. Third, inconsistent casing across files confuses imports and conventions; pick a casing style per language and stick to it — Python uses snake_case for files and CamelCase for classes. Fourth, embedding versions in filenames is unnecessary because source control manages version history. Fifth, creating 'God' classes or big utils files signals that responsibilities need to be divided. A misconception to check is that shorter names are always better. The real criterion is clarity. To avoid these mistakes, use the one-sentence responsibility test, keep files aligned to primary content, and prefer domain-driven names. Let's summarize the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, name classes as nouns or noun phrases that reveal the entity or domain concept. Second, apply the Single Responsibility Principle when naming: a name should map to a single reason to change. Third, choose interface and abstract names that read as contracts, separating them conceptually from implementations. These three points are the core of naming discipline and will shape how you navigate and maintain code. A quick self-check is to state a class's responsibility in one sentence; if you cannot, rename or split. This habit reduces friction in code reviews and accelerates onboarding.
